subject: Economy
sub_topic: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation — DICGC

concepts.name: Statutory Foundation and Institutional Character of DICGC
key_dimensions: DICGC Act, 1961 — parent legislation and its key provisions
Wholly-owned subsidiary of RBI vs. independent regulator distinction
Evolution from Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962) + Credit Guarantee Corporation (1971) merger in 1978
UPSC trap: DICGC is NOT a department of RBI but a separate legal entity under RBI umbrella

concepts.name: Coverage Limit: ₹5 Lakh Insurance per Depositor per Bank
key_dimensions: Historical progression of coverage limits: ₹1,500 (1962) → ₹1 lakh (1993) → ₹5 lakh (2020)
Coverage is per depositor per bank, NOT per account — aggregation rule
₹5 lakh covers both principal AND interest combined, not separately
UPSC trap: a depositor with ₹3 lakh in two branches of the same bank gets ₹5 lakh max, not ₹6 lakh

concepts.name: Types of Deposits Covered vs. Not Covered by DICGC
key_dimensions: Covered: savings, fixed, current, recurring deposits in insured banks
NOT covered: deposits of foreign governments, Central/State governments, inter-bank deposits, deposits outside India
NOT covered: deposits specifically exempted by RBI with DICGC concurrence
UPSC trap: State government deposits are NOT insured — only Central government deposits are excluded along with State government deposits

concepts.name: Mandatory vs. Voluntary Insurance — Which Banks Must Register
key_dimensions: All commercial banks including foreign bank branches in India are mandatorily insured
State, Central, and Primary Cooperative Banks eligible but registration mechanics differ
Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are mandatorily covered
UPSC trap: Primary cooperative societies are NOT covered; only primary cooperative BANKS are eligible

concepts.name: Premium Structure and Who Bears the Cost
key_dimensions: Premium paid entirely by insured banks, NOT passed on to depositors by law
Current premium rate: 12 paise per ₹100 of assessable deposits per annum (revised from 10 paise in 2020)
Premium is calculated on assessable deposits (total insurable deposits), not just covered portion
Risk-based premium system consideration vs. flat-rate system — policy debate angle

concepts.name: Trigger Events for DICGC Claim Payment — Liquidation vs. Restructuring
key_dimensions: Traditional trigger: cancellation of bank's licence or winding-up order
DICGC (Amendment) Act, 2021 — new trigger: bank placed under RBI Directions (moratorium) for 90 days
Post-2021: depositors can claim within 90 days of moratorium without waiting for liquidation
UPSC trap: the 2021 amendment was a paradigm shift — payment no longer waits for final liquidation

concepts.name: DICGC (Amendment) Act, 2021 — Key Reforms
key_dimensions: Introduced time-bound payment within 90 days of bank being placed under All-Inclusive Directions
Context: Punjab & Maharashtra Co-operative Bank (PMC) crisis exposing gaps in old framework
DICGC must pay insured amount even if reconstruction/amalgamation scheme is pending
Depositors receiving interim payment must assign their claim rights to DICGC (subrogation principle)

concepts.name: Credit Guarantee Function of DICGC
key_dimensions: DICGC guarantees credit to small-scale industries, small traders, small borrowers through lending institutions
Overlap and distinction with Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE)
DICGC's credit guarantee schemes have been largely transferred/wound down over time — current status awareness
UPSC trap: DICGC's name includes 'Credit Guarantee' but its active primary function today is deposit insurance

concepts.name: Role of RBI in DICGC Governance and Oversight
key_dimensions: RBI appoints DICGC Board — Chairman is typically a Deputy Governor of RBI
RBI provides lines of credit to DICGC if Deposit Insurance Fund is insufficient
RBI's power to de-register a bank from DICGC coverage and implications
Conflict of interest debate: RBI as both bank regulator and owner of deposit insurer

concepts.name: Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) — Adequacy and Management
key_dimensions: DIF built from premiums collected, investments in government securities, and recoveries from liquidated banks
Reserve ratio concept: DIF balance as % of total insured deposits — India's ratio vs. international benchmarks (e.g., FDIC's 1.35% DRR)
Concern: DIF adequacy in case of simultaneous failure of multiple large banks (systemic risk)
UPSC angle: DIF is NOT backed by explicit government guarantee (unlike US FDIC which has Treasury backing)

concepts.name: Treatment of Joint Account Holders Under DICGC
key_dimensions: Joint accounts treated as a separate depositor from individual accounts of same persons
Each permutation of joint account holders is treated as a distinct depositor
Example: A+B joint account and B+A joint account — treated as SAME depositor (same combination)
Maximizing coverage strategy: individual + joint accounts can together exceed ₹5 lakh for same person

concepts.name: International Comparisons — FDIC (USA) and Other Deposit Insurance Schemes
key_dimensions: US FDIC: $250,000 coverage, explicit government backstop, risk-based premiums — contrast with DICGC
International Association of Deposit Insurers (IADI) Core Principles — India's compliance status
Coverage ratio comparison: % of depositors fully covered (India covers ~98% of depositor accounts but only ~50% of deposit value)
UPSC angle: India's ₹5 lakh limit praised as significant improvement but deposit value coverage ratio still debated

concepts.name: Exclusion of Cooperative Societies from DICGC Coverage — Policy Gap
key_dimensions: Multi-state cooperative societies regulated by Centre; single-state by states — jurisdictional complexity
Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are NOT covered — large rural depositor vulnerability
PMC Bank crisis: highlighted gaps in cooperative bank oversight intersecting with deposit insurance
State governments' role in protecting depositors in non-DICGC-covered cooperative societies

concepts.name: Subrogation Rights of DICGC Post-Payment
key_dimensions: Once DICGC pays insured depositors, it steps into their shoes as creditor of the failed bank
DICGC's recovery rank in liquidation proceedings — where it stands in creditor hierarchy
Practical recovery rates are low — DICGC often recovers a fraction of what it pays out
UPSC trap: subrogation means depositors' claims above ₹5 lakh are NOT extinguished — they can still claim uninsured portion from liquidation estate

concepts.name: Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks — DICGC Coverage
key_dimensions: Small Finance Banks are licensed commercial banks — mandatorily covered by DICGC
Payment Banks: can accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh — also covered under DICGC
UPSC trap: Payment Banks deposit limit (₹2 lakh) is LESS than DICGC coverage limit (₹5 lakh) — so Payment Bank depositors are 100% covered
Policy significance: DICGC coverage makes Payment Banks more credible for financial inclusion goals

concepts.name: Moral Hazard Problem in Deposit Insurance Design
key_dimensions: Full coverage encourages depositor complacency — reduced market discipline on risky banks
Banks may take excessive risks knowing deposits are insured (risk-shifting to DICGC/taxpayers)
Mitigants: co-insurance (depositor bears partial loss), risk-based premiums, coverage limits
India's policy balance: broad coverage for financial inclusion vs. moral hazard containment

concepts.name: DICGC's Role in Financial Stability and Systemic Risk Mitigation
key_dimensions: Deposit insurance prevents bank runs by assuring small depositors — systemic stability function
Limited to individual bank failures — NOT a tool for addressing systemic banking crises
Interaction with Resolution Corporation concept (FRDI Bill, 2017) — proposed replacement/supplement
UPSC angle: FRDI Bill's controversial 'bail-in' clause vs. DICGC's protection — why FRDI was withdrawn

concepts.name: Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance (FRDI) Bill, 2017 — Contrast with DICGC
key_dimensions: FRDI proposed a Resolution Corporation to supersede DICGC for resolution of financial firms
Controversial 'bail-in' provision: bank could use depositor funds beyond insured limit for resolution
Bill withdrawn in 2018 amid public backlash; DICGC framework retained and strengthened instead
UPSC trap: FRDI was NOT passed; 2021 DICGC Amendment is the actual reform that materialized

concepts.name: Assessable Deposits vs. Insured Deposits — Calculation Methodology
key_dimensions: Assessable deposits = total deposits eligible for insurance (before applying ₹5 lakh cap)
Insured deposits = portion of assessable deposits actually covered after applying per-depositor cap
Premium is levied on assessable deposits; DIF liability is on insured deposits — distinction matters
Banks must submit half-yearly returns to DICGC declaring assessable deposit figures

concepts.name: De-registration of Banks from DICGC and Its Consequences
key_dimensions: RBI can cancel a bank's registration with DICGC if bank fails to pay premium or submit returns
Depositors of de-registered bank: claims for deposits made BEFORE de-registration date are still protected
Deposits made AFTER de-registration date are NOT insured — depositor awareness issue
UPSC trap: de-registration is different from licence cancellation — a bank can be de-registered from DICGC while still operational
